officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: You can explain high-side versus low-side current sensing, size a shunt for a 60 A pack, talk about coulomb counting versus voltage estimation, and show a discharge curve with a weak cell visible in it. That is battery-management experience, and 'BMS' shows up in nearly every drone, EV and robotics hardware posting.
officialData.jobMapping: Battery / power systems engineer — BMS, power monitoring and energy estimation for electric aircraft. SAFETY WARNING Never leave a LiPo connected to a discharge load unattended, and stop any test the moment a cell reads under 3.0 V — over-discharged cells are the ones that catch fire on the next charge. ## how it works ▸ Shunt plus amplifier is the whole current sensor: V = I·R, and a milliohm shunt keeps the loss to a few watts at full throttle while a dedicated current-sense amplifier rejects the common-mode voltage of the pack. ▸ Cell voltages come from differences: each balance tap is measured to ground, then cell n is tap n minus tap n−1 — which is why ADC resolution and matched dividers matter more the higher the cell. ▸ Voltage lies under load: a pack at 14.8 V resting can read 13.6 V at full throttle from internal resistance alone, which is why voltage alarms trip early and coulomb counting is what real power modules use. ▸ A weak cell hides at rest: all four cells read 4.1 V on the bench and one dips to 3.2 V under load; per-cell logging under load is how you find it before it ends a flight. flight control · motor drive · rf links · power — a Build List field guide 14 / 20
officialData.safety: Never leave a LiPo connected to a discharge load unattended, and stop any test the moment a cell reads under 3.0 V — over-discharged cells are the ones that catch fire on the next charge. ## how it works ▸ Shunt plus amplifier is the whole current sensor: V = I·R, and a milliohm shunt keeps the loss to a few watts at full throttle while a dedicated current-sense amplifier rejects the common-mode voltage of the pack. ▸ Cell voltages come from differences: each balance tap is measured to ground, then cell n is tap n minus tap n−1 — which is why ADC resolution and matched dividers matter more the higher the cell. ▸ Voltage lies under load: a pack at 14.8 V resting can read 13.6 V at full throttle from internal resistance alone, which is why voltage alarms trip early and coulomb counting is what real power modules use. ▸ A weak cell hides at rest: all four cells read 4.1 V on the bench and one dips to 3.2 V under load; per-cell logging under load is how you find it before it ends a flight. flight control · motor drive · rf links · power — a Build List field guide 14 / 20 --- PAGE 15 --- ▸ mAh used is the honest fuel gauge: integrate current, compare to rated capacity, and land at 80 % — that is exactly the rule ArduPilot and PX4 power modules enforce. ## key design decisions → Why a dedicated current-sense amplifier instead of an op-amp?: an INA240 rejects 80 dB of common-mode voltage and PWM switching noise at the shunt; a generic op-amp divider on a 16.8 V rail gives you millivolts of error on a millivolt signal. → Why a 16-bit external ADC instead of the MCU's 12-bit ADC?: 4.2 V per cell through a divider into 12 bits gives ~5 mV steps; the ADS1115 gives sub-millivolt resolution, which is what you need to see a cell drift. → Why low-side shunt here?: it keeps the amplifier referenced to ground and is how most hobby power modules are built; high-side sensing is the production answer when the ground path must stay unbroken — mention both. ## bill of materials component part / spec qty ~cost Shunt 1 m� 2512 current-sense resistor, 3 W 2 $1 Current amplifier INA240A2 (50 V/V) or INA181 breakout 1 $3 ADC ADS1115 16-bit I2C breakout 1 $3 Microcontroller + display ESP32 + 0.96-inch OLED + buzzer 1 set $7 Connectors XT60 pair, JST-XH balance lead set $2 ## build steps 1 Size the shunt for 60 A peak and a 75 mV full-scale amplifier input, choose 1 m� (60 mV at 60 A, 3.6 W peak — use a 2512 current-sense resistor rated 3 W or two in parallel) and an INA240 or INA181 amplifier with 50 V/V gain into the ADC. 2 Build the cell-voltage stage a resistor divider from each balance-lead tap (1S…4S) to an ADS1115 16-bit ADC, scaled so 4.2 V per cell lands below 3.3 V full scale, and compute per-cell voltage as the difference between adjacent taps. 3 Step 3 Calibrate against a bench meter at 0, 5 and 20 A and at three known voltages — store the slope and offset in flash, not in a comment. flight control · motor drive · rf links · power — a Build List field guide 15 / 20 --- PAGE 16 --- 4 Step 4 Integrate current at 100 Hz into mAh consumed, display pack voltage, lowest cell and mAh on a 0.96-inch OLED, and drive a buzzer when mAh used hits 80 % of rated capacity or any cell drops under 3.5 V under load. 5 Step 5 Log a full discharge on a bench load (or a tethered prop-off motor run) at 10 A and keep the curve — pack voltage, each cell, and mAh versus time. ## interview questions → How did you size the shunt and what does it dissipate at full throttle? → Why is per-cell voltage a difference measurement? → Why is a voltage alarm a bad fuel gauge? → What did your discharge curve show that a single voltage reading would not? → Where would you put the shunt in a production airframe and why? flight control · motor drive · rf links · power — a Build List field guide 16 / 20

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: You can explain two-way ranging and why it cancels clock offset, what limits UWB accuracy indoors (antenna delay, multipath, geometry), how trilateration degrades when anchors are nearly collinear, and you have a plot of a walked square that looks like a square. Localization and sensor fusion are exactly what indoor-drone companies screen for — and this build is the first rung of it.
officialData.jobMapping: Localization / navigation engineer — GPS-denied positioning and sensor fusion for indoor UAS. ## how it works ▸ Time of flight, not signal strength: UWB sends a 2 ns pulse and measures when it comes back; 1 ns of timing error is 30 cm, which is why the DW1000 timestamps to ~15 ps. ▸ Two-way ranging cancels clocks: tag sends, anchor replies after a known delay, tag times the round trip — neither side needs a synchronized clock, only a stable one. ▸ Antenna delay is the calibration: the chip timestamps at the transceiver, but the signal spends extra nanoseconds in the PCB trace and antenna; that fixed delay is subtracted per module and is why uncalibrated modules read 30–50 cm long. ▸ Geometry sets the error: three anchors in a line cannot tell which side of the line you are on; spread them around the volume and the same ranging error gives a far smaller position error (dilution of precision). ▸ Multipath is the indoor enemy: a pulse that bounces off a metal shelf arrives late and reads long; the DW1000 reports first-path power so you can reject ranges that came in via a wall. ## key design decisions flight control · motor drive · rf links · power — a Build List field guide 17 / 20
officialData.safety: Desconectar hélices y cargas antes del test inicial. Verificar polaridad y limitación de corriente en la fuente.

keyProjects.title: GOES Full-Disk Earth Receiver (1.7 GHz)
keyProjects.description: Descarga imágenes completas de la Tierra en tiempo real desde el satélite GOES a 36.000 km.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: : You understand L-band RF, low-noise amplifier and noise-figure design, link budgets, antenna gain, and digital demodulation of a BPSK downlink. These are the exact skills behind satellite communications, GPS, radar, and every space-to-ground link in the industry. --- PAGE 3 --- @1nska • 6 EE Projects That Reach Space • Page 3 How It Works • Geostationary downlink (1.69 GHz): GOES-East (GOES-19) and GOES-West (GOES-18) broadcast HRIT near 1694.1 MHz. The signal is BPSK at roughly 400 kSym/s and carries full-disk Earth images, regional mesoscale scans, and weather products. • Antenna — gain is everything: After a 36,000 km path the signal is extremely weak, so you need directional gain. A repurposed 2.4 GHz WiFi grid dish, a small offset satellite dish with a helical feed, or a DIY cookware reflector all work. Because the bird is geostationary, you point once and bolt it down. • Low-noise amplifier + SAW filter: An LNA with a sub-1 dB noise figure, mounted right at the antenna feed, sets the system sensitivity. A SAW filter near 1.69 GHz rejects cellular and WiFi that would otherwise desensitize the receiver. This LNA-at-the-antenna placement is the single most important decision in the build. • Bias tee + SDR: A bias tee injects DC up the coax to power the LNA at the mast while passing RF down to the radio. An RTL-SDR (or Airspy for more headroom) digitizes the filtered signal and streams IQ samples to a laptop or Raspberry Pi. • Demodulation + decode (SatDump): SatDump locks the BPSK carrier, recovers symbol timing, applies Viterbi and Reed-Solomon forward error correction, and reassembles the packets into full-disk and mesoscale images — the same pictures meteorologists use, pulled out of the air by you. mountingNotes: Fijación mecánica rígida: En proyectos de control inercial o sensores de movimiento, fijar la PCB con separadores M2.5 o M3 con arandelas de goma antivibración.

steps: Paso 1: Test de primer encendido seguro con fuente de laboratorio limitada a 150 mA para proteger contra cortocircuitos accidentales.
Paso 2: Ejecución de un escáner de bus (ej. I2C Scanner) para verificar que el periférico responde en su dirección hex esperada.
Paso 3: Protocolo de reposo estático (Zero-Motion Calibration): Mantener el dispositivo inmóvil sobre una superficie nivelada durante 5 segundos para calcular y restar el sesgo estático (bias).
Paso 4: Validación de rango dinámico: Aplicar estímulos conocidos y verificar mediante el Serial Plotter que la señal responde sin saturación ni ruido espurio.
Paso 5: Calibración de tiempo muerto y seguridad de desconexión (Failsafe timeout): Comprobar que el sistema entra en modo seguro si se interrumpe la comunicación por más de 100 ms.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: El microcontrolador no detecta el módulo o el bus se congela aleatoriamente.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Ausencia de resistencias pull-up adecuadas o cableado demasiado largo con capacitancia parasita > 400 pF.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Añadir resistencias pull-up externas de 2.2 kΩ a 4.7 kΩ entre las líneas SDA/SCL y el riel de 3.3V, y acortar los cables a menos de 10 cm.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Reinicios esporádicos del microcontrolador (Brown-out Reset) al arrancar actuadores o transmisores.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Caída brusca de tensión provocada por el pico de corriente de arranque (inrush current) del periférico.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Soldar un condensador electrolítico de baja ESR de 470 µF a 1000 µF en paralelo con el riel de potencia y alimentar la etapa de potencia mediante una fuente independiente con masa común.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Ruido excesivo o deriva continua en la señal adquirida.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Acoplamiento electromagnético procedente de motores o falta de filtrado cerámico de alta frecuencia en la alimentación.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Colocar un condensador cerámico SMD de 100 nF lo más cerca posible de los pines VDD y GND del sensor, y habilitar un filtro paso bajo digital (DLPF) en el firmware.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Sobrecalentamiento del regulador de voltaje LDO o del circuito integrado.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Disipación de potencia excesiva por caída de tensión elevada (ej. alimentar un chip de 3.3V desde 12V a través de un regulador lineal).
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Reemplazar el LDO lineal por un convertidor reductor conmutado (Buck DC-DC) de alta eficiencia o añadir un disipador de aluminio.

keyProjects.title: Meteor-M2 Weather Satellite Receiver (137 MHz)
keyProjects.description: Recepción de fotos de alta resolución de tu ciudad con antena V-dipole casera.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: : You understand VHF reception, antenna design and polarization (why satellites use circular polarization), Doppler shift, and digital QPSK demodulation with forward error correction — the same RF fundamentals that scale all the way up to GOES and deep-space communication. --- PAGE 7 --- @1nska • 6 EE Projects That Reach Space • Page 7 How It Works • Polar LRPT downlink (137 MHz): Meteor-M2-3 and M2-4 transmit LRPT near 137.9 MHz (137.1 MHz backup). Unlike the old analog NOAA APT, LRPT is digital QPSK at about 72 kbps, carrying a crisper multi-spectral image. • A satellite that moves: These satellites orbit roughly 800 km up in a sun-synchronous polar orbit, crossing your sky in about 12–15 minutes per pass. You capture a strip of Earth directly under the ground track — typically your region and a few hundred km either side. • Antenna and polarization: A V-dipole (two ~50 cm wires at about 120 degrees) is the simplest antenna; a QFH (quadrifilar helix) is omnidirectional and better for the ever-changing pass geometry. Satellites transmit circular polarization, which is why a QFH outperforms a flat dipole on low passes. • Optional LNA for the city: In a quiet rural spot the SDR alone can decode a high pass. In a city full of RF noise, a 137 MHz SAW-filtered LNA at the antenna dramatically improves results by rejecting pagers, FM broadcast, and other interference. • Doppler and decode (SatDump): Because the satellite is moving fast, its frequency shifts by several kHz across the pass (Doppler). SatDump tracks the satellite by its orbital elements, corrects Doppler, demodulates the QPSK, applies error correction, and assembles the decoded image. keyProjects.title: Reaction-Wheel Attitude Controller
keyProjects.description: Rueda de reacción balanceada que orienta una plataforma espacial mediante conservación de momento.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: : You understand closed-loop control (PID/LQR), sensor fusion, BLDC motor torque control, and real-time embedded firmware. Attitude determination and control is a core aerospace discipline, and the same fundamentals underpin robotics, drones, and self-balancing vehicles. --- PAGE 10 --- @1nska • 6 EE Projects That Reach Space • Page 10 How It Works • Conservation of angular momentum: The platform sits on a low-friction bearing. When the motor accelerates the flywheel clockwise, the platform reacts by rotating counter-clockwise. The torque on the body equals the rate of change of the wheel's angular momentum — so wheel acceleration is your control input. • IMU attitude sensing: An MPU-6050 or BNO055 IMU fuses its gyroscope and accelerometer to estimate the platform's tilt angle and angular rate. A complementary or Kalman filter blends the drift-free-but-noisy accelerometer with the smooth-but-drifting gyro. • The control loop: A PID (or LQR) controller takes the angle error and computes a commanded wheel torque. For the balancing-pendulum version it must stabilize an inherently unstable equilibrium — like balancing a broom on your palm, but a thousand times a second. • BLDC torque control: A brushless gimbal motor spins the flywheel. A field-oriented control (FOC) driver regulates motor current, and since torque is proportional to current, this gives direct, smooth torque control — far better than crude PWM speed control. • Momentum saturation: If the platform keeps disturbing in one direction, the wheel spins faster and faster until it hits its limit — saturation. Real satellites dump this momentum with magnetorquers or thrusters. On the bench you will watch the wheel max out and learn why momentum management matters. fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Ausencia de resistencias pull-up adecuadas o cableado demasiado largo con capacitancia parasita > 400 pF.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Reinicios esporádicos del microcontrolador (Brown-out Reset) al arrancar actuadores o transmisores.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Caída brusca de tensión provocada por el pico de corriente de arranque (inrush current) del periférico.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Ruido excesivo o deriva continua en la señal adquirida.

keyProjects.title: Camera-Based Star Tracker
keyProjects.description: Cámara que identifica constelaciones nocturnas y calcula la orientación absoluta de la nave.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: : You understand low-light image sensors and optics (f-number, exposure), embedded computer vision, star-identification algorithms, and the coordinate-frame math (quaternions) behind pointing systems. Star trackers are flagship aerospace GNC hardware — building one signals you can work on real spacecraft guidance. --- PAGE 13 --- @1nska • 6 EE Projects That Reach Space • Page 13 How It Works • Fast lens + low-light sensor: Stars are dim, so the optics matter most. A fast lens (f/1.4–f/2) gathers maximum light; a sensitive CMOS sensor (a Raspberry Pi HQ camera or a Sony IMX module) with a multi-second exposure captures enough stars per frame to identify a pattern. Monochrome and longer exposure both help. • Star centroiding: The software thresholds the image to separate stars from background, then computes the sub-pixel centroid of each star blob. Centroiding to a fraction of a pixel is what gives the tracker its arc-second accuracy — far finer than the pixel grid itself. • Pattern matching (lost in space): The key trick: the angular distances between stars form a unique fingerprint. An open-source solver like Tetra3 hashes these geometric patterns and matches them against a precomputed catalog — identifying exactly which stars you are looking at with no prior orientation estimate. • Attitude solve: Once stars are identified, their known catalog positions (right ascension and declination) plus their measured pixel positions let the solver compute the rotation that maps one to the other. The result is the camera's orientation, expressed as a quaternion or rotation matrix. • Edge compute: All of this runs on a Raspberry Pi (Zero 2 W or Pi 4). The solve takes well under a second per frame — fast enough to output a continuous attitude estimate, exactly as a real star tracker feeds a spacecraft's control system. keyProjects.title: GPS-Disciplined Oscillator (GPSDO)
keyProjects.description: Reloj de referencia de 10 MHz con precisión atómica sincronizado con la señal PPS de GPS.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: : You understand precision frequency references, phase-locked control loops, GNSS timing (1PPS), oscillator steering via DAC or varactor, and how to characterize stability with Allan deviation. Timing and synchronization is foundational to communications, radar, and instrumentation — and surprisingly few engineers actually understand it. --- PAGE 16 --- @1nska • 6 EE Projects That Reach Space • Page 16 How It Works • The 1PPS reference: A GPS receiver outputs a one-pulse-per-second signal whose rising edge is aligned to GPS system time — itself steered by the atomic clocks aboard the satellites. The edge is accurate to tens of nanoseconds, but it jitters pulse-to-pulse, so it is a great long-term reference and a poor short-term one. • The local oscillator: An OCXO (oven-controlled crystal oscillator) is extremely stable second-to-second but slowly drifts over hours and temperature. It is the opposite of GPS: great short-term, poor long-term. The whole idea is to combine the two. • Phase comparison: The MCU divides the OCXO (e.g. 10 MHz) down to 1 Hz and measures the time error between that and the GPS 1PPS using a hardware timer's input capture. This error, in nanoseconds, is the signal the control loop drives to zero. • The loop filter: A slow software control loop — a long time constant of many seconds to minutes — averages out the GPS jitter and computes a correction. Too fast and you chase GPS noise; too slow and you fail to track drift. This tradeoff is the heart of the design. • Steering the oscillator: The correction drives a DAC that sets the OCXO's electronic frequency control (EFC) voltage, nudging it a few parts-per-billion. Over minutes the loop converges and the OCXO is disciplined — its frequency now traceable to the same standard as the satellites overhead. keyProjects.title: Cosmic-Ray Muon Detector
keyProjects.description: Detector de partículas subatómicas del espacio profundo mediante fotomultiplicador de silicio.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: : You understand SiPM biasing and temperature compensation, low-noise transimpedance amplification, fast pulse discrimination, and coincidence detection. This is high-speed, low-noise analog at the edge of what is possible — exactly the skill set behind medical imaging, LIDAR, and scientific instrumentation. --- PAGE 19 --- @1nska • 6 EE Projects That Reach Space • Page 19 How It Works • The scintillator: A block of plastic scintillator (cast PVT, or a surplus offcut) emits a brief flash of blue light when a charged particle deposits energy crossing it. A single muon produces only a few hundred to a few thousand photons — faint and fast, lasting nanoseconds. • Silicon photomultiplier (SiPM): A SiPM is an array of avalanche photodiodes biased just above breakdown, giving enormous gain (around 106) — enough to turn a handful of photons into a measurable current pulse. It replaces the bulky, high-voltage photomultiplier tubes of old with a 6 mm chip running on about 29 V. • Precise bias + temperature: A SiPM's gain is steeply sensitive to bias voltage and temperature, so a stable, low-noise bias supply (a quiet boost converter plus filtering) is critical. Drift the voltage and your count rate drifts with it — which is why real systems add temperature compensation. • Fast amplifier: A transimpedance or voltage amplifier with enough bandwidth (tens of MHz) converts the SiPM's fast current spike into a clean voltage pulse without smearing it. Layout matters here — short traces, good grounding, and supply bypassing keep noise below the tiny signal. • Discrimination and counting: A comparator fires when a pulse exceeds a threshold set just above the noise floor, producing a clean digital tick per event. An MCU counts ticks and shows the muon rate on an OLED. Add a second detector and require coincidence — only count when both fire at once — to reject electrical noise and confirm real through-going particles. officialData.whatThisProves: You understand photoplethysmography, separating a small AC signal riding on a large DC baseline, band-pass filtering, peak detection, and why motion artifacts dominate wearable sensing — the core of consumer health-device engineering.

officialData.safety: . It is not a medical instrument. Real SpO₂ readings require empirical calibration against a clinical reference on actual subjects — a number your build cannot produce trustworthily. Never make a health decision from it, and if you are worried about your heart or breathing, see a doctor, not a breadboard. reading the body — a Build List field guide 2 / 20 --- PAGE 3 --- ## how it works ## bill of materials component part / spec qty ~cost PPG sensor module MAX30102 (red + IR + photodiode) 1 $5 Microcontroller ESP32 / Arduino (I2C) 1 $8 Display (optional) OLED for live waveform 1 $4 Passives + breadboard wiring — $2 Light in, blood out: An LED sends light into the tissue and a photodiode measures how much comes back. Blood volume rises with each heartbeat and absorbs more light, so the detected signal dips in time with your pulse. ▸ AC riding on DC: Most of what the photodiode sees is constant — skin, bone, static blood. The heartbeat is a tiny fluctuation (the AC part) on top of that big DC level. Extracting a clean AC from a dominant DC is the whole game. ▸ Why green for heart rate: Green light is strongly absorbed by haemoglobin and penetrates shallowly, giving a strong pulse signal with less motion sensitivity. That is why fitness wearables glow green on your wrist. ▸ Red and infrared for oxygenation: Oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin absorb red (~660 nm) and infrared (~940 nm) light differently. Comparing the pulsatile signal at both wavelengths is how commercial pulse oximeters estimate SpO₂ — but only after calibration against a clinical reference. ▸ Band-pass and peak detect: A heart rate lives around 0.7–3 Hz (40–180 bpm). Band-pass the signal into that window to kill DC drift and high-frequency noise, then detect peaks and time the intervals to get beats per minute. ▸ reading the body — a Build List field guide 3 / 20 --- PAGE 4 --- ## build steps ## interview questions Read the raw sensor Wire the MAX30102 over I2C, load the library, and stream the raw red and IR counts. Rest a fingertip on it and confirm the numbers wobble slightly with each heartbeat. 1 Plot the waveform Stream the raw values to a plot. You should see a large baseline with a small ripple — that ripple is your pulse. Note how much bigger the DC part is than the AC part. 2 Filter to the pulse band Band-pass roughly 0.7–3 Hz to remove the DC baseline and high-frequency noise. The waveform should now show clean, repeating pulse peaks. 3 Count the beats Detect peaks, measure the interval between them, and convert to beats per minute. Compare to your pulse counted by hand at the wrist to sanity-check the number. 4 Break it on purpose Move your finger, press harder, press lighter, and watch the signal collapse into motion artifact. Understanding why wearables struggle during exercise is the real lesson here. 5 What physical effect does a PPG sensor actually measure? → Why is the pulsatile part of a PPG signal so small compared to the baseline? → Why do fitness wearables use green light for heart rate? → How do red and infrared light let a pulse oximeter estimate oxygenation? → Why can a DIY SpO₂ reading not be trusted without calibration? → What causes motion artifacts in PPG, and how would you reduce them? → reading the body — a Build List field guide 4 / 20

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: You understand instrumentation-amplifier topology, common-mode rejection (CMRR), driven- reference (right-leg drive) circuits, electrode half-cell offsets and why you must AC- couple, gain staging, and mains-hum rejection — the foundation of all precision biomedical analog design.
officialData.jobMapping: medical-device and precision-analog engineering — patient-monitoring, diagnostics, and analog front-end teams.
officialData.safety: , ALWAYS — AND NEVER INJECT CURRENT Anything wired to your skin must run on batteries and must never be connected to mains- powered gear (a plugged-in laptop, a bench scope, a wall adapter) while electrodes are on a body. Use series resistors in every electrode lead, and isolate (Bluetooth, or an unplugged battery laptop) if you need to see the data on a computer. Everything in this guide only measures — never build anything that pushes current into a person, and do not attach electrodes to anyone with a pacemaker or implanted device. reading the body — a Build List field guide 5 / 20 --- PAGE 6 --- ## how it works ## bill of materials component part / spec qty ~cost Instrumentation amp INA333 or AD620 1 $6 Op-amp for driven reference + filters (quad) 1 $2 Ag/AgCl electrodes disposable snap electrodes (pack) 1 $6 Passives + breadboard resistors, caps, lead resistors — $4 Batteries 9 V pair (isolated supply) 2 $3 The signal is tiny, the noise is huge: An ECG is about 1 mV, an EMG a few mV, an EEG only tens of microvolts. Meanwhile your body couples capacitively to mains wiring and carries volts of 50 / 60 Hz interference. The signal is buried a thousandfold. ▸ Differential rescue: That interference appears almost identically on both measuring electrodes (it is common-mode), while the biosignal appears as a difference between them. An instrumentation amplifier amplifies the difference and rejects the common part — its ability to do so is its CMRR. ▸ Driven reference (right-leg drive): Better still, sense the common-mode voltage on the body, invert it, and feed it back through a third electrode. This actively cancels the interference at the source and buys you far more rejection than the amplifier alone — without ever tying the body to ground. ▸ Electrode offsets force AC coupling: Two Ag/AgCl electrodes on skin produce a DC half-cell voltage of up to a few hundred millivolts — hundreds of times bigger than the signal. If you applied full gain to that, the amplifier would slam into its rail. So you take modest gain first, high-pass to strip the DC, then apply the rest of the gain. ▸ Filtering to the band you want: Each biosignal has a band: ECG roughly 0.5–40 Hz, EMG roughly 20–450 Hz, EEG roughly 1–30 Hz. Band-pass to that window (plus an optional 50 / 60 Hz notch) and you throw away most of the remaining noise. ▸ reading the body — a Build List field guide 6 / 20 --- PAGE 7 --- ## build steps ## interview questions Build the amplifier core Wire the instrumentation amp with a modest first-stage gain (about 10). Power it from batteries only. Test it with a signal generator or a divider before it ever touches skin. 1 Add series lead resistors Put a current-limiting resistor (tens of kΩ) in each electrode lead. This is a safety measure, not an optional extra, and it costs you nothing in signal quality. 2 AC-couple and add gain High-pass at roughly 0.5 Hz to strip the electrode DC offset, then add a second gain stage (100 or more) plus a low-pass for your band. Confirm the output no longer saturates. 3 Add the driven reference Buffer and invert the common-mode voltage and drive it back into a third electrode on a bony spot (hip or elbow). Watch the mains hum on your output collapse — this is the most satisfying moment in the build. 4 Prove it on a real signal Put two electrodes across your forearm, clench your fist, and watch the burst of muscle activity. You now have the front end that every remaining project in this guide depends on. 5 Why is an instrumentation amplifier used instead of a single op-amp for biopotentials? → What is CMRR, and why does it dominate biosignal front-end design? → How does a driven-reference (right-leg drive) circuit improve noise rejection? → Why must a biopotential amplifier be AC-coupled before high gain? → Why is the gain split across stages instead of applied all at once? → Why must a body-connected circuit be battery powered and isolated? → reading the body — a Build List field guide 7 / 20

officialData.whatThisProves: You understand cardiac electrophysiology at the signal level, lead configurations, the ECG bandwidth, R-peak detection algorithms, heart-rate and HRV extraction, and safe patient-connected design — the exact skill set of medical-device and patient-monitoring engineering.

officialData.safety: , not a diagnostic tool. It is not calibrated, not validated, and not certified. It can show you a waveform and a heart rate; it cannot tell you whether your heart is healthy, and a normal-looking trace means nothing clinically. Never make a health decision from it. If you have any cardiac concern, see a doctor. reading the body — a Build List field guide 8 / 20 --- PAGE 9 --- ## how it works BUILD NOTE The AD8232 packages the whole front end — instrumentation amp, right-leg drive, and filters — into one $10 chip. Start there to get a waveform fast, then rebuild it with your project-2 front end to prove you understand what the chip is doing. ## key design decisions The heart as a moving dipole: As the cardiac muscle depolarises, it creates an electrical wavefront that behaves like a rotating dipole in your torso. Electrodes on the skin see the projection of that dipole — which is why where you place them changes what you see. ▸ Reading the PQRST: The P wave is atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex is the much larger ventricular depolarisation, and the T wave is ventricular repolarisation. Their shapes and timings are what clinicians read; for you, the tall R peak is the easiest landmark. ▸ Leads and placement: Einthoven’s triangle defines the classic limb leads. Lead I runs right arm to left arm; Lead II (right arm to left leg) usually gives the biggest, cleanest R peak — a good first target. A third electrode carries the driven reference. ▸ The right bandwidth: Monitoring-grade ECG lives roughly between 0.5 and 40 Hz. Band-pass there and you remove electrode drift below and muscle noise above, without mangling the QRS shape. ▸ Finding the beats: The classic R-peak detector (Pan-Tompkins) band-passes the signal, differentiates it, squares it, integrates over a moving window, and thresholds the result. Time the intervals between R peaks and you have heart rate and beat-to-beat variability. ▸ Why not just notch out the mains hum and skip the fancy front end? A notch filter removes interference after the amplifier — but if the hum is a thousand times larger than the signal, it has already saturated your gain stages and the ECG is unrecoverable. And a notch near the QRS band distorts the waveform. The real fix is rejecting the interference at the input, with CMRR and a driven reference, so it never gets amplified in the first place. → Why drive a reference electrode instead of just grounding the body? Tying a person to circuit ground creates a low-impedance path for fault current — a safety hazard — and it does not actually cancel the common-mode voltage. A driven-reference electrode feeds back an inverted copy of the common-mode signal through a high-value resistor, actively cancelling the hum while keeping the connection current-limited and safe. → Why AC-couple when the ECG has low-frequency content? Electrode half-cell offsets reach hundreds of millivolts against a 1 mV signal, so without a high-pass the amplifier rails and you see nothing at all. The compromise is to set the corner low (about 0.5 Hz) — enough to strip electrode drift while preserving the ECG’s slow features like the T wave. → reading the body — a Build List field guide 9 / 20 --- PAGE 10 --- ## bill of materials component part / spec qty ~cost ECG front end AD8232 module (or your project-2 front end) 1 $10 Ag/AgCl electrodes disposable snap electrodes (pack) 1 $6 Microcontroller ESP32 / Arduino (ADC) 1 $8 Battery 9 V or LiPo (isolated supply) 1 $3 Passives lead resistors, wiring — $2 ## build steps Wire it up on battery Connect the front end and microcontroller and power the whole thing from a battery. Confirm it works before an electrode ever touches you, and keep it disconnected from any mains-powered device. 1 Place three electrodes Two measuring electrodes (Lead I across the arms, or Lead II for a bigger R peak) and one driven reference on a bony landmark. Clean the skin so the contact is good — poor contact ruins everything downstream. 2 Get a raw trace Stream the ADC values and plot them. Sit very still. You should see a repeating waveform with an unmistakable sharp spike — your QRS complex. Move and watch it drown in artifact. 3 Filter and clean up Band-pass roughly 0.5–40 Hz and, if needed, notch the mains frequency. The P, QRS, and T features should now be clearly separable on the plot. 4 Detect beats and compute rate Implement R-peak detection, compute beats per minute from the R-R intervals, and display it. Compare to your pulse counted by hand, then watch the rate rise after a set of push- ups. 5 reading the body — a Build List field guide 10 / 20

steps: Paso 1: Test de primer encendido seguro con fuente de laboratorio limitada a 150 mA para proteger contra cortocircuitos accidentales.
Paso 2: Ejecución de un escáner de bus (ej. I2C Scanner) para verificar que el periférico responde en su dirección hex esperada.
Paso 3: Protocolo de reposo estático (Zero-Motion Calibration): Mantener el dispositivo inmóvil sobre una superficie nivelada durante 5 segundos para calcular y restar el sesgo estático (bias).
Paso 4: Validación de rango dinámico: Aplicar estímulos conocidos y verificar mediante el Serial Plotter que la señal responde sin saturación ni ruido espurio.
Paso 5: Calibración de tiempo muerto y seguridad de desconexión (Failsafe timeout): Comprobar que el sistema entra en modo seguro si se interrumpe la comunicación por más de 100 ms.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: El microcontrolador no detecta el módulo o el bus se congela aleatoriamente.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Ausencia de resistencias pull-up adecuadas o cableado demasiado largo con capacitancia parasita > 400 pF.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Añadir resistencias pull-up externas de 2.2 kΩ a 4.7 kΩ entre las líneas SDA/SCL y el riel de 3.3V, y acortar los cables a menos de 10 cm.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Reinicios esporádicos del microcontrolador (Brown-out Reset) al arrancar actuadores o transmisores.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Caída brusca de tensión provocada por el pico de corriente de arranque (inrush current) del periférico.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Soldar un condensador electrolítico de baja ESR de 470 µF a 1000 µF en paralelo con el riel de potencia y alimentar la etapa de potencia mediante una fuente independiente con masa común.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Ruido excesivo o deriva continua en la señal adquirida.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Acoplamiento electromagnético procedente de motores o falta de filtrado cerámico de alta frecuencia en la alimentación.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Colocar un condensador cerámico SMD de 100 nF lo más cerca posible de los pines VDD y GND del sensor, y habilitar un filtro paso bajo digital (DLPF) en el firmware.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Sobrecalentamiento del regulador de voltaje LDO o del circuito integrado.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Disipación de potencia excesiva por caída de tensión elevada (ej. alimentar un chip de 3.3V desde 12V a través de un regulador lineal).
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Reemplazar el LDO lineal por un convertidor reductor conmutado (Buck DC-DC) de alta eficiencia o añadir un disipador de aluminio.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: You understand surface EMG generation, why its band differs from ECG, envelope detection (rectify plus low-pass), electrode placement along muscle fibres, crosstalk between adjacent muscles, and turning a biosignal into a usable control value — the basis of human-machine interface work.
officialData.jobMapping: biomedical sensing and human-machine interface engineering — neural- wearable, rehab-tech, and gesture-input teams. ## how it works Where the signal comes from: A motor neuron fires and the muscle fibres it controls depolarise. Thousands of these overlapping action potentials sum into a noisy, spiky voltage at the skin — a few hundred microvolts to a few millivolts, much rougher-looking than an ECG. ▸ A different band: Most EMG energy sits between about 20 and 450 Hz. High-passing at ~20 Hz is essential: it rejects motion artifact and the ECG contamination that would otherwise pollute a recording taken anywhere near the torso. ▸ The envelope is the useful part: Raw EMG looks like noise, and its instantaneous value is meaningless for control. Rectify it (take the absolute value) and low-pass it, and you get a smooth envelope whose height tracks contraction strength — that is the signal you actually use. ▸ Placement and crosstalk: Put two electrodes on the belly of the target muscle, aligned with the fibre direction, with a reference on a bony landmark. Place them poorly and you will pick up neighbouring muscles — crosstalk, the main reason multi-gesture control is hard. ▸ Fatigue and drift: As a muscle tires, the EMG amplitude and frequency content shift, so a fixed threshold that worked ten minutes ago may not work now. Real systems recalibrate or normalise — a lesson that matters immediately in project 5. ▸ reading the body — a Build List field guide 12 / 20

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: You can design a genuinely low-noise, high-gain analog front end, manage shielding and grounding at the microvolt level, distinguish real neural signal from muscle and eye artifact, and validate a result experimentally. Microvolt-level analog design and honest artifact rejection are precisely what neurotech teams look for.
officialData.jobMapping: neurotech and brain-computer interface engineering — BCI startups, neural-wearable companies, and neuroscience research labs.
officialData.safety: — a rhythm that appears when your eyes close and disappears when they open — is the realistic and honest goal. Anything claiming to read thoughts or emotions from a few electrodes is overselling. Most hobby “brainwave” projects are actually detecting jaw clenching or eye blinks; the eyes-closed alpha test is how you prove yours is real. This is also not a diagnostic device, and it cannot tell you anything about your neurological health. reading the body — a Build List field guide 17 / 20 --- PAGE 18 --- ## how it works BUILD NOTE This is the one build where sloppiness guarantees failure. Battery power, shielded leads, short wires, a driven reference, and real electrode contact (gold cup electrodes with conductive paste, parted through the hair) are not optional extras — they are the difference between alpha waves and a screen full of mains hum. ## bill of materials component part / spec qty ~cost Low-noise front end INA333 (or ADS1299 for the serious build) 1 $8 Precision op-amps filters + driven reference 1 $5 Gold cup electrodes + paste occipital, reference, ground 1 $20 Shielded cable + enclosure short shielded leads, metal box — $8 ADC / microcontroller 24-bit ADC or ESP32 + care 1 $10 Batteries + passives isolated supply, filters — $9 Microvolts, not millivolts: Scalp EEG is roughly 10–100 µV — ten to a hundred times smaller than an ECG. That means much higher gain (often 10,000× or more), far lower noise, and no tolerance for the sloppy wiring you got away with earlier. ▸ The alpha rhythm: When a relaxed person closes their eyes, neurons in the visual cortex synchronise into an 8–12 Hz oscillation that is strongest over the occipital region, at the back of the head. Opening the eyes suppresses it almost immediately. This alpha blocking is the classic, reproducible EEG demonstration. ▸ Electrodes and placement: Measure over the occipital area, referenced to an earlobe or mastoid, with a driven reference electrode. Gold cup electrodes with conductive paste (parted through the hair) give far better contact than dry electrodes — and contact quality dominates your result. ▸ Artifacts everywhere: Eye blinks produce huge slow deflections, jaw and neck tension produce broadband muscle noise, and any cable movement produces artifact. All of these are bigger than the alpha you are chasing, which is why so many “brainwave” demos are really artifact detectors. ▸ Proving it with an FFT: Band-pass roughly 1–30 Hz, run an FFT, and watch the power in the 8–12 Hz bin. Eyes closed and relaxed: it rises. Eyes open: it drops. Toggling that on command, repeatably, is your proof the signal is neural and not noise. ▸ reading the body — a Build List field guide 18 / 20 --- PAGE 19 --- ## build steps ## interview questions Build for noise, not speed Assemble the front end with very high gain, split across stages, band-passed to about 1– 30 Hz with a mains notch. Keep leads short and shielded and run everything from batteries in a shielded enclosure. 1 Prove the rig on ECG first Before you go near your head, record an ECG with the same rig. If you cannot get a clean ECG, you will never see EEG — this step will save you a weekend of confusion. 2 Place occipital electrodes Part the hair and apply gold cup electrodes with paste over the occipital region, reference on the earlobe or mastoid, plus the driven reference. Check contact impedance; poor contact is the number one failure. 3 Sit still, close your eyes Relax, stay very still, and record with eyes closed for thirty seconds, then eyes open for thirty seconds. Stillness matters enormously — any jaw tension will swamp the signal. 4 Find the alpha in the FFT Run an FFT and compare the 8–12 Hz band power between the two conditions. A clear rise with eyes closed, repeatable across trials, is real alpha. Anything that only appears when you blink or clench is artifact — be honest about which you got. 5 Why is EEG so much harder to measure than ECG? → What is the alpha rhythm, and what causes alpha blocking? → Why is electrode contact impedance so critical in EEG? → What are the dominant artifacts in EEG, and how do you identify them? → How would you prove that a signal you recorded is neural and not muscle artifact? → What are the realistic limits of a low-channel-count EEG system? → reading the body — a Build List field guide 19 / 20

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: You understand photodiode and phototransistor detection, turning a light level into a clean logic edge with a comparator, microsecond-scale timing on a microcontroller, and converting a time interval into a physical measurement — the core of optical sensing and instrumentation.
officialData.jobMapping: optical sensing & instrumentation — industrial automation, robotics, and test-and-measurement teams.
officialData.safety: . Use only low-power Class 1 / 2 modules (a few mW), never look into the beam or aim it at anyone, and remember infrared lasers are invisible — you cannot tell they are on. Set beams below eye level and keep this in mind for every build in this guide. seeing with light — a Build List field guide 2 / 18 --- PAGE 3 --- ## how it works ## bill of materials component part / spec qty ~cost Laser diode module 5 mW red dot laser (×2) 2 $4 Photodiode / phototransistor BPW34 or a phototransistor (×2) 2 $2 Comparator LM393 (dual) 1 $1 Microcontroller Arduino / ESP32 1 $8 Passives + breadboard resistors, wiring — $3 Light to current: A photodiode (or phototransistor) turns incident light into a small current. A laser aimed at it holds that current high; break the beam and it collapses. A load resistor turns the current into a voltage you can read. ▸ Clean edge with a comparator: The raw photodiode voltage is analog and noisy. A comparator (or Schmitt trigger) with a threshold turns “beam present / broken” into a crisp digital edge — immune to ambient drift — that a microcontroller can timestamp. ▸ Two beams, one interval: Place two beams a measured distance d apart along the path. The object breaks beam A, then beam B; the microcontroller measures Δt between the two edges. Speed = d / Δt. ▸ Microsecond timing: For a fast projectile, Δt is sub-millisecond, so you use hardware timers and interrupts (input capture), not slow polling. The resolution of your timer sets the resolution of your speed. ▸ Rejecting ambient light: Sunlight and room light add a DC offset and flicker. A focused laser well above the ambient level, a threshold set between the two, and a shielded detector keep the beam-break reliable indoors and out. ▸ seeing with light — a Build List field guide 3 / 18

fase2_wiring.busNotes: El bus I2C debe mantenerse con cables de menos de 15 cm para evitar capacitancia parasita excesiva. Si se comparten múltiples sensores, verificar que no haya colisión de direcciones I2C (ej. 0x68 vs 0x69).

mountingNotes: Fijación mecánica rígida: En proyectos de control inercial o sensores de movimiento, fijar la PCB con separadores M2.5 o M3 con arandelas de goma antivibración.
Orientación de los ejes: Alinear el eje X del sensor serigrafiado en la placa con el vector de avance o puntería del dispositivo.
Gestión térmica: Colocar pequeños disipadores autoadhesivos de aluminio en el procesador y chips de potencia si el consumo supera los 500 mW.
Carcasa y blindaje: Diseñar o imprimir en 3D la carcasa en filamento PETG o ABS para resistencia mecánica y térmica en exteriores.

steps: Paso 1: Test de primer encendido seguro con fuente de laboratorio limitada a 150 mA para proteger contra cortocircuitos accidentales.
Paso 2: Ejecución de un escáner de bus (ej. I2C Scanner) para verificar que el periférico responde en su dirección hex esperada.
Paso 3: Protocolo de reposo estático (Zero-Motion Calibration): Mantener el dispositivo inmóvil sobre una superficie nivelada durante 5 segundos para calcular y restar el sesgo estático (bias).
Paso 4: Validación de rango dinámico: Aplicar estímulos conocidos y verificar mediante el Serial Plotter que la señal responde sin saturación ni ruido espurio.
Paso 5: Calibración de tiempo muerto y seguridad de desconexión (Failsafe timeout): Comprobar que el sistema entra en modo seguro si se interrumpe la comunicación por más de 100 ms.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: El microcontrolador no detecta el módulo o el bus se congela aleatoriamente.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Ausencia de resistencias pull-up adecuadas o cableado demasiado largo con capacitancia parasita > 400 pF.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Añadir resistencias pull-up externas de 2.2 kΩ a 4.7 kΩ entre las líneas SDA/SCL y el riel de 3.3V, y acortar los cables a menos de 10 cm.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Reinicios esporádicos del microcontrolador (Brown-out Reset) al arrancar actuadores o transmisores.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Caída brusca de tensión provocada por el pico de corriente de arranque (inrush current) del periférico.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Soldar un condensador electrolítico de baja ESR de 470 µF a 1000 µF en paralelo con el riel de potencia y alimentar la etapa de potencia mediante una fuente independiente con masa común.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Ruido excesivo o deriva continua en la señal adquirida.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Acoplamiento electromagnético procedente de motores o falta de filtrado cerámico de alta frecuencia en la alimentación.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Colocar un condensador cerámico SMD de 100 nF lo más cerca posible de los pines VDD y GND del sensor, y habilitar un filtro paso bajo digital (DLPF) en el firmware.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Sobrecalentamiento del regulador de voltaje LDO o del circuito integrado.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Disipación de potencia excesiva por caída de tensión elevada (ej. alimentar un chip de 3.3V desde 12V a través de un regulador lineal).
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Reemplazar el LDO lineal por un convertidor reductor conmutado (Buck DC-DC) de alta eficiencia o añadir un disipador de aluminio.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: You understand synchronising a sensor reading to an angular position, polar-to-Cartesian conversion, point-cloud construction, and the data path from a raw sensor to a usable map — foundational robotics-perception and SLAM groundwork.
officialData.jobMapping: robotics, autonomous navigation, and perception engineering — robot- vacuum and AMR makers, drone companies, and SLAM teams. ## how it works BUILD NOTE Don’t machine a precision scanner. A stepper (or geared DC motor with an encoder) plus your project-2 ToF module is enough; send data off the spinning platform over a slip ring, or mount the electronics on the rotor and stream over BLE / Wi-Fi. Distance plus angle: A LiDAR map is just many (angle, distance) pairs. Rotate the ToF sensor and, at each angle, take a reading. The accuracy of your angle (from the motor) and distance (from the sensor) sets the quality of the map. ▸ Knowing the angle: A stepper gives you angle for free (count steps); a DC motor needs an encoder or a once-per-revolution index mark to know where “zero” is. Synchronising each distance sample to the correct angle is the core challenge. ▸ Getting data off the spinner: Either run a slip ring for power and data, or — simpler — put the microcontroller and sensor on the rotating platform and stream readings out over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, with only power crossing the slip ring (or a battery onboard). ▸ Polar to Cartesian: Each (θ, r) becomes a point x = r·cosθ, y = r·sinθ. Plotting all the points for one revolution draws the walls and objects around the sensor — your 2D point cloud. ▸ From scan to map: Stack revolutions and you can filter noise, detect walls, and (with motion) start stitching scans together — the first step toward SLAM, where a robot builds a map while tracking its own position. ▸ seeing with light — a Build List field guide 8 / 18

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: You understand intensity modulation of an optical source, transimpedance photodiode receivers, bandwidth and signal-to-noise in an analog link, and the basics of free-space optics — which maps onto optical-comms, fibre, and photonics engineering.
officialData.jobMapping: optical communications and photonics engineering — fibre and datacom companies, free-space-optics and satellite-comms teams. ## how it works Intensity modulation: The simplest optical link varies the laser’s brightness in step with your signal. For audio, you add the audio to the laser’s drive current so the light flickers with the waveform; a photodiode on the far end sees that flicker. ▸ The transimpedance receiver: The photodiode produces a tiny current proportional to received light. A transimpedance amplifier (op-amp + feedback resistor) converts it to a usable voltage with enough bandwidth for your signal — the heart of every optical receiver. ▸ Analog vs digital: Sending audio (analog AM on light) is the easy first version. Sending digital data (on-off keying, UART over light) is the next step: now you care about bit rate, thresholding, and clean edges rather than fidelity. ▸ Bandwidth, and why light wins: The optical carrier is hundreds of terahertz, so the available bandwidth dwarfs radio — which is why fibre and laser links carry so much data. Your build’s actual speed is limited by the emitter and receiver electronics, not the light. ▸ Alignment and noise: A tight beam makes the link private and interference-resistant, but you must aim it. Ambient light adds noise and offset, so you AC-couple the receiver (and modulate above the flicker of room lights) to keep the signal clean. ▸ seeing with light — a Build List field guide 10 / 18

steps: Paso 1: Test de primer encendido seguro con fuente de laboratorio limitada a 150 mA para proteger contra cortocircuitos accidentales.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: El microcontrolador no detecta el módulo o el bus se congela aleatoriamente.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Ausencia de resistencias pull-up adecuadas o cableado demasiado largo con capacitancia parasita > 400 pF.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Añadir resistencias pull-up externas de 2.2 kΩ a 4.7 kΩ entre las líneas SDA/SCL y el riel de 3.3V, y acortar los cables a menos de 10 cm.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Reinicios esporádicos del microcontrolador (Brown-out Reset) al arrancar actuadores o transmisores.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Caída brusca de tensión provocada por el pico de corriente de arranque (inrush current) del periférico.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Soldar un condensador electrolítico de baja ESR de 470 µF a 1000 µF en paralelo con el riel de potencia y alimentar la etapa de potencia mediante una fuente independiente con masa común.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Ruido excesivo o deriva continua en la señal adquirida.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Acoplamiento electromagnético procedente de motores o falta de filtrado cerámico de alta frecuencia en la alimentación.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Colocar un condensador cerámico SMD de 100 nF lo más cerca posible de los pines VDD y GND del sensor, y habilitar un filtro paso bajo digital (DLPF) en el firmware.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Sobrecalentamiento del regulador de voltaje LDO o del circuito integrado.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Disipación de potencia excesiva por caída de tensión elevada (ej. alimentar un chip de 3.3V desde 12V a través de un regulador lineal).
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Reemplazar el LDO lineal por un convertidor reductor conmutado (Buck DC-DC) de alta eficiencia o añadir un disipador de aluminio.

officialData.safety: -sensing technique for surfaces and devices you own — a speaker cone, a motor housing, a panel on your own bench. Do not point it at other people’s windows, rooms, or property to capture sound or conversations: that is eavesdropping, it is illegal in most places, and it is not what this build is for. Keep it on your own equipment. seeing with light — a Build List field guide 12 / 18 --- PAGE 13 --- ## how it works ## bill of materials component part / spec qty ~cost Laser module 5 mW red dot laser 1 $3 Photodiode BPW34 or similar 1 $2 Low-noise amp op-amp + band-pass stage 1 $3 Capture audio interface or ESP32 ADC 1 $8 Mounts / optics rigid stands, small mirror, your own test surface — $6 Light carries surface motion: When a laser reflects off a surface, the reflected beam’s direction and the light coupled back into your detector depend on the surface’s exact position. Vibrate the surface and the photodiode sees a matching AC signal riding on the reflection. ▸ The detector geometry: A simple setup catches the reflected dot at the edge of a photodiode (or through a slit) so small angular shifts change how much light lands on the sensor — converting tiny surface motions into a measurable voltage swing. ▸ Recovering a tiny signal: The vibration signal is small and sits on a large DC level from the steady reflection. AC-coupling, a low-noise amplifier, and band-pass filtering pull the vibration (an audio-band signal from a speaker, say) out of the background. ▸ Why it is hard: The signal depends heavily on surface reflectivity, alignment, and ambient light, and it is easily swamped by noise or a poor reflector. Stable mounting and a cooperative, shiny target are what make it work. ▸ What the pros do: True laser Doppler vibrometers interfere the reflected beam with a reference to read sub-wavelength motion precisely. Your build is the intuition-level version of that instrument — same idea, far simpler optics. ▸ seeing with light — a Build List field guide 13 / 18

keyProjects.title: 10.5 GHz Doppler Motion Radar
keyProjects.description: Detección de velocidad y movimiento en microondas con módulo Gunn HB100.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: You understand the Doppler effect, continuous-wave radar, mixing down to baseband, low- noise audio amplification, and basic FFT-based spectral estimation on a microcontroller — the literal core of radar signal processing.
officialData.jobMapping: radar & sensing engineering — automotive, security / occupancy sensing, and defense radar groups. ## how it works Continuous-wave Doppler: The HB100 transmits an unmodulated ~10.525 GHz carrier and mixes the returning echo with it. A stationary target returns the same frequency (zero beat); a moving target returns a Doppler-shifted frequency, and the mixer outputs the difference — a low audio tone. ▸ The Doppler equation: The beat frequency is fd = 2·v·f₀/c. At 10.5 GHz, every 1 m/s of radial speed produces ~70 Hz of beat, so walking speed (~1.5 m/s) lands near 100 Hz — squarely in the audio band, which is why a cheap op-amp can handle it. ▸ Amplifying microvolts: The raw IF output is tiny (microvolts to millivolts) and low- frequency. A two-stage op-amp with band-pass shaping (roughly 20 Hz–3 kHz) lifts it to a clean line level the ADC can read, while rejecting DC offset and mains hum. ▸ Sampling and the FFT: An Arduino or ESP32 samples the amplified beat at a few kHz and runs an FFT. The peak bin is the dominant Doppler frequency; convert it back to m/s with the equation and you have a live speed readout. ▸ Reading direction (bonus): A plain HB100 cannot tell approaching from receding (both shift the magnitude up). Modules with I/Q outputs, or an added quadrature mixer, recover the sign of the shift — the same trick higher-end Doppler sensors use. ▸ seeing with radio — a Build List field guide 2 / 19

keyProjects.description: Pistola de velocidad con lectura digital directa en km/h o mph para coches y pelotas.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: You can take a raw sensor and turn it into a calibrated instrument — fixed-point conversion, peak detection and hold, display integration, and validating a measurement against a known reference. That instrumentation discipline is exactly what test-and- measurement and sensor teams hire for.
officialData.jobMapping: measurement & instrumentation, test engineering, and embedded sensor roles — sporting-tech, automotive test, and T&M companies. ## how it works From beat frequency to mph: The conversion is fixed: speed = fd·c / (2·f₀). Precompute the constant for your module’s exact frequency so each FFT peak maps directly to km/h or mph with one multiply — fast enough to update several times a second. ▸ Peak detection and hold: A passing target’s speed peaks then fades as the geometry changes. The firmware tracks the maximum valid reading over a short window and “holds” it on the display — exactly how a real speed gun reports the fastest moment of a pitch or a car. ▸ Cosine (angle) error: Doppler measures only the velocity component along the beam. Aim off- axis by angle θ and the reading is low by cos θ. Aiming nearly head-on keeps the error tiny — and explains why speed traps are aimed straight down the road. ▸ Antenna gain and range: The bare module sees a few metres. Putting it at the focus of a cheap parabolic or horn (or even a metal can) narrows the beam and adds gain, extending useful range and rejecting off-axis clutter — a tangible lesson in antenna directivity. ▸ Display and packaging: An OLED or 7-segment shows the held speed; a momentary button re- arms it. Mounting the module, amp, MCU, and display in a 3D-printed grip turns the breadboard into something that reads as a real device on camera. ▸ seeing with radio — a Build List field guide 5 / 19

prepChecklist: Inspeccionar visualmente todos los pines del MCU y módulos para descartar puentes de soldadura.
Verificar con el multímetro en modo continuidad la ausencia total de cortocircuito entre VCC y GND antes de encender.
Comprobar que la tensión de alimentación del riel lógico no exceda el límite del chip (máx 3.6V para ESP32 / Cortex-M).
Tener preparado el cable de datos USB apantallado y el entorno de compilación (Arduino IDE / PlatformIO / Python 3).

wiringTable.note: Riel regulado de bajo ruido; añadir condensador de 100nF cerca del pin VCC.
Plano de masa común con retorno directo al MCU.
Línea bidireccional de datos con resistencia pull-up de 4.7 kΩ a 3.3V.
Línea de reloj síncrono hasta 400 kHz (Fast Mode) con pull-up de 4.7 kΩ.
Flanco de subida para Data-Ready; evita polling innecesario en la CPU.

fase2_wiring.busNotes: El bus I2C debe mantenerse con cables de menos de 15 cm para evitar capacitancia parasita excesiva. Si se comparten múltiples sensores, verificar que no haya colisión de direcciones I2C (ej. 0x68 vs 0x69).

mountingNotes: Fijación mecánica rígida: En proyectos de control inercial o sensores de movimiento, fijar la PCB con separadores M2.5 o M3 con arandelas de goma antivibración.
Orientación de los ejes: Alinear el eje X del sensor serigrafiado en la placa con el vector de avance o puntería del dispositivo.
Gestión térmica: Colocar pequeños disipadores autoadhesivos de aluminio en el procesador y chips de potencia si el consumo supera los 500 mW.
Carcasa y blindaje: Diseñar o imprimir en 3D la carcasa en filamento PETG o ABS para resistencia mecánica y térmica en exteriores.

fase4_firmware.loopRate: 250 Hz (4 milisegundos por iteración) sincronizado por interrupción de temporizador
fase4_firmware.algorithm: Arquitectura cíclica determinista con muestreo regularizado por interrupciones de hardware, desacoplando el tiempo de lectura del tiempo de procesamiento y envío.

steps: Paso 1: Test de primer encendido seguro con fuente de laboratorio limitada a 150 mA para proteger contra cortocircuitos accidentales.
Paso 2: Ejecución de un escáner de bus (ej. I2C Scanner) para verificar que el periférico responde en su dirección hex esperada.
Paso 3: Protocolo de reposo estático (Zero-Motion Calibration): Mantener el dispositivo inmóvil sobre una superficie nivelada durante 5 segundos para calcular y restar el sesgo estático (bias).
Paso 4: Validación de rango dinámico: Aplicar estímulos conocidos y verificar mediante el Serial Plotter que la señal responde sin saturación ni ruido espurio.
Paso 5: Calibración de tiempo muerto y seguridad de desconexión (Failsafe timeout): Comprobar que el sistema entra en modo seguro si se interrumpe la comunicación por más de 100 ms.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: El microcontrolador no detecta el módulo o el bus se congela aleatoriamente.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Ausencia de resistencias pull-up adecuadas o cableado demasiado largo con capacitancia parasita > 400 pF.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Añadir resistencias pull-up externas de 2.2 kΩ a 4.7 kΩ entre las líneas SDA/SCL y el riel de 3.3V, y acortar los cables a menos de 10 cm.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Reinicios esporádicos del microcontrolador (Brown-out Reset) al arrancar actuadores o transmisores.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Caída brusca de tensión provocada por el pico de corriente de arranque (inrush current) del periférico.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Soldar un condensador electrolítico de baja ESR de 470 µF a 1000 µF en paralelo con el riel de potencia y alimentar la etapa de potencia mediante una fuente independiente con masa común.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Ruido excesivo o deriva continua en la señal adquirida.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Acoplamiento electromagnético procedente de motores o falta de filtrado cerámico de alta frecuencia en la alimentación.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Colocar un condensador cerámico SMD de 100 nF lo más cerca posible de los pines VDD y GND del sensor, y habilitar un filtro paso bajo digital (DLPF) en el firmware.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Sobrecalentamiento del regulador de voltaje LDO o del circuito integrado.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Disipación de potencia excesiva por caída de tensión elevada (ej. alimentar un chip de 3.3V desde 12V a través de un regulador lineal).
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Reemplazar el LDO lineal por un convertidor reductor conmutado (Buck DC-DC) de alta eficiencia o añadir un disipador de aluminio.

keyProjects.description: Detección de personas a través de paredes analizando las perturbaciones CSI de Wi-Fi.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Es el bloque fundamental que diferencia a un aficionado de un ingeniero profesional: control determinista, análisis de tolerancias y fiabilidad en campo.
officialData.whatThisProves: You understand phase / quadrature processing, micro-Doppler signatures, narrow-band filtering to separate physiological rhythms, and the limits of motion-based sensing. This phase-domain RF skill set maps onto biomedical sensing, gesture / presence radar, and the mmWave presence-sensing products shipping today.
officialData.jobMapping: biomedical and contactless-sensing engineering — medical-device R&D, gesture / presence radar teams, and health-tech startups.
officialData.safety: -Doppler sensing, not a medical instrument. It can show a breathing and pulse rhythm on a plot; it is not validated, not safe to rely on, and must never be used to make a health decision or to diagnose anyone. Treat it as physics you can see — not a monitor. seeing with radio — a Build List field guide 10 / 19 --- PAGE 11 --- ## how it works ## bill of materials component part / spec qty ~cost I/Q Doppler module HB100 (basic) or CDM324 / I-Q 24 GHz sensor 1 $4–15 Low-noise amp dual op-amp, low offset 1 $2 ADC / MCU ESP32 or audio interface to PC 1 $8 Passives + breadboard filters, wiring — $5 Micro-Doppler from tiny motion: A chest moving even a millimetre changes the radar path length, which shifts the echo’s phase. Breathing moves the chest ~4–12 mm; a heartbeat ~0.2–0.5 mm. Both appear as slow phase modulation on the returned signal. ▸ Quadrature (I/Q) phase: Reliable extraction needs I and Q channels so you track phase directly rather than amplitude. A module with I/Q outputs (or an added quadrature mixer) lets you compute the small chest displacement over time. ▸ Separating breath from heartbeat: Respiration sits around 0.1–0.5 Hz and cardiac around 0.8–2 Hz. Two band-pass filters split the combined motion into a respiration waveform and a much smaller cardiac waveform you can rate-count. ▸ Why it is hard: The heartbeat signal is tiny and easily buried by body motion and breathing harmonics. The subject must be still; averaging over several seconds and rejecting large motions is what makes the pulse emerge. ▸ Reading the rates: FFT or peak-interval analysis on each filtered band gives breaths-per- minute and beats-per-minute. Plotting the two waveforms live is the demo: a slow rise-and- fall for breathing, a faster ripple for the heart. ▸ seeing with radio — a Build List field guide 11 / 19

mountingNotes: Fijación mecánica rígida: En proyectos de control inercial o sensores de movimiento, fijar la PCB con separadores M2.5 o M3 con arandelas de goma antivibración.
Orientación de los ejes: Alinear el eje X del sensor serigrafiado en la placa con el vector de avance o puntería del dispositivo.
Gestión térmica: Colocar pequeños disipadores autoadhesivos de aluminio en el procesador y chips de potencia si el consumo supera los 500 mW.

fase4_firmware.loopRate: 250 Hz (4 milisegundos por iteración) sincronizado por interrupción de temporizador
fase4_firmware.algorithm: Arquitectura cíclica determinista con muestreo regularizado por interrupciones de hardware, desacoplando el tiempo de lectura del tiempo de procesamiento y envío.

steps: Paso 1: Test de primer encendido seguro con fuente de laboratorio limitada a 150 mA para proteger contra cortocircuitos accidentales.
Paso 2: Ejecución de un escáner de bus (ej. I2C Scanner) para verificar que el periférico responde en su dirección hex esperada.
Paso 3: Protocolo de reposo estático (Zero-Motion Calibration): Mantener el dispositivo inmóvil sobre una superficie nivelada durante 5 segundos para calcular y restar el sesgo estático (bias).
Paso 4: Validación de rango dinámico: Aplicar estímulos conocidos y verificar mediante el Serial Plotter que la señal responde sin saturación ni ruido espurio.
Paso 5: Calibración de tiempo muerto y seguridad de desconexión (Failsafe timeout): Comprobar que el sistema entra en modo seguro si se interrumpe la comunicación por más de 100 ms.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: El microcontrolador no detecta el módulo o el bus se congela aleatoriamente.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Ausencia de resistencias pull-up adecuadas o cableado demasiado largo con capacitancia parasita > 400 pF.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Añadir resistencias pull-up externas de 2.2 kΩ a 4.7 kΩ entre las líneas SDA/SCL y el riel de 3.3V, y acortar los cables a menos de 10 cm.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Reinicios esporádicos del microcontrolador (Brown-out Reset) al arrancar actuadores o transmisores.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Caída brusca de tensión provocada por el pico de corriente de arranque (inrush current) del periférico.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Soldar un condensador electrolítico de baja ESR de 470 µF a 1000 µF en paralelo con el riel de potencia y alimentar la etapa de potencia mediante una fuente independiente con masa común.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Ruido excesivo o deriva continua en la señal adquirida.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Acoplamiento electromagnético procedente de motores o falta de filtrado cerámico de alta frecuencia en la alimentación.
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Colocar un condensador cerámico SMD de 100 nF lo más cerca posible de los pines VDD y GND del sensor, y habilitar un filtro paso bajo digital (DLPF) en el firmware.

fase6_troubleshooting.symptom: Sobrecalentamiento del regulador de voltaje LDO o del circuito integrado.
fase6_troubleshooting.cause: Disipación de potencia excesiva por caída de tensión elevada (ej. alimentar un chip de 3.3V desde 12V a través de un regulador lineal).
fase6_troubleshooting.fix: Reemplazar el LDO lineal por un convertidor reductor conmutado (Buck DC-DC) de alta eficiencia o añadir un disipador de aluminio.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Every ship, aircraft, drone, and vehicle depends on GNSS for position and precise time, which makes it one of the most important — and most contested — signals in defense. Building a receiver is the way in: a $12 module locks onto satellites 20,000 km overhead and hands you latitude, longitude, altitude, and nanosecond-grade time, and with an SDR you can even glimpse the raw signal buried below the noise floor. Understanding how GNSS works, and why it is so fragile, is foundational to positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) engineering — one of the largest and most strategically vital areas of defense EE. defense signals — a Build List field guide 2 / 17 --- PAGE 3 ---
officialData.whatThisProves: You understand GNSS fundamentals (trilateration from time-of-flight, the role of precise time), NMEA data, why the signal sits below the noise floor and how correlation recovers it, and the concepts of jamming and spoofing resilience. PNT is core defense and aerospace EE.
officialData.jobMapping: positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) engineering — aerospace, defense, autonomous-systems, and timing-infrastructure teams.
officialData.safety: — NEVER JAM OR SPOOF This build only listens. Jamming or spoofing GNSS is a serious federal crime and endangers aircraft, ships, and emergency services, so nothing here transmits and the resilience discussion stays conceptual. Understanding the threat is a defensive skill; creating it is not.

officialData.whyThisMatters: Finding where a radio signal comes from is one of the oldest and most important jobs in defense electronics — search and rescue, spectrum enforcement, electronic warfare, and signals intelligence all rest on it. Build a direction finder and you can watch a bearing swing to point straight at a hidden transmitter across a field. The accessible version uses a single SDR with a directional antenna and signal strength, or a pseudo-Doppler array; the serious version uses a coherent multi- channel SDR to compute true angle-of-arrival from phase. It is the marquee build of this guide — visual, deeply technical, and a direct window into how SIGINT and EW systems locate emitters. defense signals — a Build List field guide 5 / 17
officialData.whatThisProves: You understand direction-finding techniques (RSSI / rotational, pseudo-Doppler, and phase- based angle-of-arrival), coherent multi-channel reception, antenna arrays, and the math that turns antenna phase differences into a bearing. Coherent RF and DF are advanced, in-demand skills across SIGINT, EW, and spectrum work.
officialData.jobMapping: signals intelligence, electronic warfare, and spectrum engineering — defense RF, spectrum-monitoring, and search-and-rescue teams.
officialData.safety: , DON'T INTRUDE This is receive-only: you locate transmitters, you never transmit or interfere. Use it for fox-hunting, tracking down interference, or search-and-rescue beacons, and respect privacy and radio law — don’t use it to covertly track people.
